passage: In the Pune flat, Gurleen curled up on the sofa with Papa's tablet and typed question after question to the AI assistant. Why do volcanoes erupt? How many legs does a spider have? The answers appeared in seconds, and she squealed each time. Her older brother Nilesh looked up from his homework. "Don't just believe it, Gurleen. Check it in the encyclopedia." Later she found one answer that didn't match her science book. She frowned, then carried both to school and asked her teacher, who showed her which to trust. Gurleen still loved asking, but she liked knowing where to check.

qa.q: What did Gurleen ask the AI assistant about?
qa.a: She asked why volcanoes erupt and how many legs a spider has.

qa.q: What was Gurleen feeling as the answers appeared, and what made her check one?
qa.a: She was delighted and curious, squealing at each answer; she checked one because it did not match her science book.

qa.q: How can Gurleen use the AI assistant for learning?
qa.a: Keep asking, then double-check with books and teachers, as she did with her science book and her teacher 🙂.

qa.q: How might Nilesh see Gurleen's questions?
qa.a: With approval for her curiosity, while nudging her to check facts in the encyclopedia rather than simply believing the assistant.

grounding: Illustrates a child curious and delighted by an AI assistant who double-checks with books and a teacher.

passage:
I'm Ramesh, and during the summer holidays I asked the AI helper on Papa's laptop about a hundred questions. Why is the sea salty? How do bats find their way? Do octopuses have hearts? Every answer came in a blink, like a genie. I loved it.
Then my friend Asif and I made a poster about octopuses for school. The AI had said an octopus has two hearts. Asif's library book said three. We stared at each other. "Who's right?" Asif asked. We showed Sultana Miss, who opened a second book. Three hearts!
Now I still ask the AI loads of things, but for school work I check with a book or a teacher too. It is still fun. It just isn't always right.

qa.q: How many hearts did Asif's library book say an octopus has?
How did Ramesh feel about the AI's instant answers at first?
qa.a: Ramesh was delighted and amazed, as if the AI were a genie.

qa.q: What habit did Ramesh build after the octopus mix-up?
qa.a: To keep asking the AI but check school facts with a book or a teacher.

qa.q: How might Asif have seen the moment the two answers clashed?
qa.a: Asif was puzzled and curious about who was right, which led them to ask Sultana Miss.

grounding: A child loves an AI assistant's instant answers and learns to double-check with books and teachers because it can be wrong.

passage:
Library period note, Friday
Kashish spent the whole period at the library computer asking the AI tool about volcanoes, one question after another, bouncing on the chair. "It answers before I finish thinking!" she told Uma. When it said the big hill outside our town was an active volcano, Uma frowned. Her uncle had climbed it many times; it was just rock.
Kashish looked unsure, so I suggested they check. Together we opened the geography atlas and a children's encyclopedia: the hill is not a volcano at all.
Kashish laughed. "So it can be wrong!" She wrote a new rule on her notebook cover: "Ask AI, then check." I have asked her to share it with the class on Monday.

qa.q: What rule did Kashish write on her notebook cover?
How did Kashish feel while asking the AI questions?
qa.a: She felt excited and delighted, bouncing on the chair because it answered so fast.

qa.q: What did the library teacher suggest, and why did it help?
qa.a: They suggested checking the atlas and encyclopedia, which showed the AI's mistake without spoiling Kashish's curiosity.

qa.q: How did Uma see the AI's answer?
qa.a: Uma doubted it, because her uncle had climbed the hill many times and knew it was just rock.

grounding: A teacher's note shows a curious girl enjoying an AI's quick answers and learning to double-check with books because it can be wrong.
